html:
A fast-ripening, drought-hardy rice that reached Song China from the kingdom of Champa in what is now central Vietnam. In 1012 Emperor Zhenzong had large amounts of its seed sent from Fujian to farmers in the lower Yangtze and Huai regions.

Its value was speed. It could ripen in as little as sixty days, so farmers in the south could grow two crops a year in the same field, and it grew on higher land that ordinary rice could not use.

Together with new dams, terraces and tools, Champa rice helped the Song feed a population that passed 100 million, the largest in the world at the time. More food meant bigger cities, more trade and a shift of China's wealth and people to the south. Similar quick crops from abroad, such as maize and the sweet potato, did the same job again under the Ming and Qing.
